# Bind mounts and mount propagation: shared, slave, private, unbindable

## Overview

**Thesis:** a bind mount makes the same directory tree visible at a second place. **Propagation** decides what happens *later*: when something is mounted or unmounted under one of those places, does the other place see it? Every mount has one propagation type, and the type answers that question. Containers, `systemd` `PrivateTmp=`, Kubernetes volume mounts (`mountPropagation:`), `chroot` build setups and "my USB stick appeared inside the container" all depend on it.

| Type | Events from peers/master arrive here | Events here go out | `/proc/self/mountinfo` tag | `findmnt -o PROPAGATION` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **shared** | yes (from peers) | yes (to peers and slaves) | `shared:N` | `shared` |
| **slave** | yes (from its master) | no | `master:N` | `private,slave` |
| shared + slave | yes | yes, to its own peers | `shared:M master:N` | `shared,slave` |
| **private** | no | no | (none) | `private` |
| **unbindable** | no | no, and it cannot be bind-mounted | `unbindable` | `private,unbindable` |

N is the **peer group** ID. Mounts with the same `shared:N` are peers. A mount with `master:N` receives from peer group N.

## Mental model

![A shared mount at a and its bind mount b form peer group 98, so a mount under either appears under both. A slave bind at c has master 98: mounts under a arrive at c, but a mount made under c stays there. A private bind at d receives nothing. An unbindable mount refuses mount --bind.](../../../images/diagram-mount-propagation.svg){fig-alt="Four boxes for the same tmpfs mounted at /tmp/proplab/a, b, c and d. a and b are linked by a two-way arrow labelled peer group shared:98, and a note says a mount at a/sub also appears at b/sub. From a to c there is a one-way arrow labelled master:98: the mount at a/two arrives at c/two, but the mount made at c/three does not travel back to a. d is private with no arrows: a/four never appears under d. A fifth box marked unbindable shows mount --bind d e failing with EINVAL. A footer notes that unshare -m makes the new namespace private by default, while --propagation unchanged keeps shared mounts shared, so mounts made in the child leak back to the parent."}

```text
        shared:98               master:98
   a  <==========>  b      a  ----------->  c        d (private)    d (unbindable)
   mount a/sub  -> b/sub   mount a/two  -> c/two     a/four: not    mount --bind d e
                           mount c/three -/-> a      seen in d      -> EINVAL
```

Three rules:

1. **Propagation belongs to the mount, not the directory.** `mount --make-*` changes the mount at that path; `--make-r*` changes it and every mount below.
2. **A bind mount copies the propagation of the source.** Bind a shared mount and the new mount joins the same peer group; that is why `b` saw `a/sub`.
3. **A new mount namespace starts as a copy.** Shared mounts stay peers *across* namespaces, so a mount made inside a "container" can show up on the host unless someone makes the tree private or slave first.

## Syntax

```bash
mount --bind  OLD NEW            # one mount, no submounts
mount --rbind OLD NEW            # the mount and everything mounted below it
mount -o bind,ro OLD NEW         # read-only view of one mount
mount -o rbind,ro=recursive OLD NEW   # read-only for the whole tree (mount_setattr, Linux >= 5.12)
mount --make-shared   PATH       # also: --make-slave, --make-private, --make-unbindable
mount --make-rshared  PATH       # recursive variants: --make-rslave, --make-rprivate, --make-runbindable
findmnt -o TARGET,SOURCE,PROPAGATION [-R PATH]
grep PATH /proc/self/mountinfo   # field 7+: shared:N master:N propagate_from:N unbindable
unshare -m [--propagation private|slave|shared|unchanged] CMD   # default: private
```

## Safety

- Every example below runs inside `unshare -rm`: a new user namespace (you are "root" there with no real privilege) plus a new mount namespace. Nothing touches the host's mount table, and everything disappears when the shell exits.
- On a real host, `--make-rprivate /` or `--make-rshared /` changes behaviour for every service. Do it only inside a namespace you created.
- `umount -l` (lazy) on a shared mount propagates the unmount to every peer and slave.

## Examples with Explanations

All examples come from one script run as `unshare -rm bash lab.sh` in `/tmp/proplab`. First, where we start:

```text
$ findmnt -no PROPAGATION /
private
```

`unshare` makes the whole tree private by default (see Notes for what a normal systemd host looks like).

### 1. Shared: two places, one peer group

```text
$ mount -t tmpfs lab a
$ mount --make-shared a
$ mount --bind a b
$ grep proplab /proc/self/mountinfo
260 242 0:38 / /tmp/proplab/a rw,relatime shared:98 - tmpfs lab rw,uid=1000,gid=1000
261 242 0:38 / /tmp/proplab/b rw,relatime shared:98 - tmpfs lab rw,uid=1000,gid=1000
$ mkdir a/sub && mount -t tmpfs one a/sub
$ findmnt -o TARGET,SOURCE,PROPAGATION -R a; findmnt -no TARGET,SOURCE,PROPAGATION -R b
TARGET               SOURCE PROPAGATION
/tmp/proplab/a       lab    shared
└─/tmp/proplab/a/sub one    shared
/tmp/proplab/b       lab shared
└─/tmp/proplab/b/sub one shared
```

`a` and `b` are the same tmpfs (device `0:38`) and both carry `shared:98`. The tmpfs mounted at `a/sub` afterwards appears at `b/sub` as well: a mount event under one peer is replayed under every peer.

### 2. Slave: receive, never send

```text
$ mount --bind a c
$ mount --make-slave c
$ mkdir -p a/two c/three
$ mount -t tmpfs two a/two
$ mount -t tmpfs three c/three
$ grep -E "proplab/(a|c)(/two|/three)? " /proc/self/mountinfo
260 242 0:38 / /tmp/proplab/a rw,relatime shared:98 - tmpfs lab rw,uid=1000,gid=1000
264 242 0:38 / /tmp/proplab/c rw,relatime master:98 - tmpfs lab rw,uid=1000,gid=1000
265 260 0:45 / /tmp/proplab/a/two rw,relatime shared:126 - tmpfs two rw,uid=1000,gid=1000
267 264 0:45 / /tmp/proplab/c/two rw,relatime master:126 - tmpfs two rw,uid=1000,gid=1000
271 264 0:48 / /tmp/proplab/c/three rw,relatime - tmpfs three rw,uid=1000,gid=1000
$ findmnt -no TARGET,SOURCE,PROPAGATION -R c
/tmp/proplab/c         lab   private,slave
├─/tmp/proplab/c/two   two   private,slave
└─/tmp/proplab/c/three three private
$ findmnt -no TARGET -R a
/tmp/proplab/a
├─/tmp/proplab/a/sub
└─/tmp/proplab/a/two
```

`c` started as another peer of 98 (rule 2), and `--make-slave` turned `shared:98` into `master:98`. Now `a/two` arrives as `c/two` (also a slave, of the new group 126), but `c/three` stays local: it has no tag, and `a`'s tree has no `three`. This is the type you want for "a container should see new host mounts, but its own mounts must not leak out". `c` has no `sub` because `--bind` copies one mount, not the ones below it (example 5).

### 3. Private: a frozen copy

```text
$ mount --bind a d
$ mount --make-private d
$ mkdir -p a/four && mount -t tmpfs four a/four
$ findmnt -no TARGET,PROPAGATION -R d
/tmp/proplab/d private
```

`d` was bound from `a` and made private. The later `a/four` never shows up in `d`.

### 4. Unbindable: no copies at all

```text
$ mount --make-unbindable d
$ mount --bind d e; echo exit=$?
mount: /tmp/proplab/e: wrong fs type, bad option, bad superblock on /tmp/proplab/d, missing codepage or helper program, or other error.
       dmesg(1) may have more information after failed mount system call.
exit=32
```

The kernel refuses with `EINVAL`, which util-linux turns into its generic "wrong fs type, bad option..." message. Unbindable mounts exist to stop the exponential mount explosion you get when a tree is recursively bound into a directory inside itself.

### 5. `--bind` vs `--rbind`

```text
$ mount --bind a e
$ mount --rbind a f
$ findmnt -no TARGET -R e | wc -l; findmnt -no TARGET -R f | wc -l
1
4
```

By now `a` has three submounts (`sub`, `two`, `four`). `--bind` copied only `a` itself; `--rbind` copied all four. For a chroot (`/dev`, `/proc`, `/sys` with their submounts) you almost always want `--rbind`, followed by `--make-rslave` so that unmounting the chroot does not unmount the host's `/dev/pts`.

### 6. Read-only binds are not recursive by default

A tmpfs `r` with a submount `r/in`, bound read-only two ways (`ro.sh`, also inside `unshare -rm`):

```text
$ mount -o rbind,ro r s; findmnt -no TARGET,OPTIONS -R s | cut -d, -f1
/tmp/proplab/s      ro
└─/tmp/proplab/s/in rw
$ mount -o rbind,ro=recursive r t; findmnt -no TARGET,OPTIONS -R t | cut -d, -f1
/tmp/proplab/t      ro
└─/tmp/proplab/t/in ro
```

Plain `ro` with `rbind` made only the top mount read-only, and `s/in` is still writable. `ro=recursive` (util-linux with the new mount API, using `mount_setattr(2)` with `AT_RECURSIVE`) covers the whole tree. If you hand a container a "read-only" host tree, check with `findmnt -o TARGET,OPTIONS -R`.

## The trap: a new mount namespace that is still shared

Same user namespace, a fresh shared mount `g`, and two child mount namespaces (`lab6.sh`):

```text
$ mount -t tmpfs host g && mount --make-shared g
$ mkdir g/x g/y
# child namespace that keeps propagation as-is:
$ unshare -m --propagation unchanged sh -c 'mount -t tmpfs leak /tmp/proplab/g/x'
# child namespace with unshare default (--propagation private):
$ unshare -m sh -c 'mount -t tmpfs safe /tmp/proplab/g/y; findmnt -no TARGET,SOURCE /tmp/proplab/g/y'
/tmp/proplab/g/y safe
# back in the parent namespace:
$ findmnt -no TARGET,SOURCE,PROPAGATION -R g
/tmp/proplab/g     host shared
└─/tmp/proplab/g/x leak shared
```

The first child kept propagation unchanged, so its `g/x` mount travelled back to the parent: a "private" namespace that was not private. The second used unshare's default and its `g/y` stayed inside. Hand-rolled container code that calls `unshare(CLONE_NEWNS)` directly gets the first behaviour, because the *syscall* does not change propagation; only the `unshare` command does, and only by default. Container runtimes call `mount("", "/", NULL, MS_REC|MS_SLAVE, NULL)` (or `MS_PRIVATE`) right after creating the namespace for exactly this reason.

One more cross-namespace rule from mount_namespaces(7): when the new mount namespace belongs to a *less privileged* user namespace, shared mounts copied from the parent become **slave** mounts, and they are locked, so the child cannot unmount them to reveal what is underneath.

## Notes and pitfalls

- **systemd makes `/` shared.** On a normal systemd host, PID 1 runs the equivalent of `mount --make-rshared /` at boot, so `findmnt -no PROPAGATION /` prints `shared`. The kernel default for new mounts is private. The machine these examples ran on is itself a container, so its `/` is `private`.
- **`findmnt` wording.** Slaves print as `private,slave`, meaning "slave, and not shared"; `/proc/self/mountinfo` is the unambiguous source.
- **Kubernetes** exposes this as `mountPropagation: None | HostToContainer | Bidirectional`, which map to private, rslave and rshared. `Bidirectional` needs a privileged container for the leak reason above.
- **Docker** has `--mount type=bind,...,bind-propagation=rslave` (default `rprivate`).
- **`PrivateTmp=` and `ProtectSystem=`** in systemd units are built from a new mount namespace with slave propagation plus bind mounts.
- **Bind-mounting a file** works too (`mount --bind file1 file2`), but editors that save by rename replace the directory entry, and the bind keeps showing the old inode.
- **Recursive read-only** needs `ro=recursive` (example 6). It relies on `mount_setattr(2)` with `AT_RECURSIVE`, which arrived in Linux 5.12.

## The boring rule

After creating a mount namespace, make it `rslave` (or `rprivate`) before mounting anything. Use `--rbind` plus `--make-rslave` for chroots. Read `/proc/self/mountinfo` when `findmnt`'s wording is unclear.

## Related Commands

- `mount` and `umount` (this part): `--bind`, `--rbind`, lazy unmounts
- `unshare` (Services and runtime part): `--propagation`
- `findmnt -o TARGET,PROPAGATION -R`, `cat /proc/self/mountinfo`
- `nsenter -t PID -m findmnt`: look at another process's mount namespace

## Try this

1. In `unshare -rm`, make `a` shared, bind it to `b`, then `umount a/sub`. Does `b/sub` disappear?
2. Build a shared+slave mount: bind a slave `c` to `h` and run `mount --make-shared c` first. What tags does `/proc/self/mountinfo` show for `c` and `h`?
3. Run `mount --rbind /tmp/proplab /tmp/proplab/a` twice, then count mounts with `findmnt -R /tmp/proplab | wc -l`. Repeat after `--make-unbindable`.
4. On a systemd machine, compare `findmnt -no PROPAGATION /` on the host and inside `systemd-run -p PrivateTmp=yes --pty findmnt -no PROPAGATION /tmp`.

## Verification

- `lab.sh`, `lab6.sh` and `ro.sh` were run inside `unshare -rm` (util-linux 2.41.5) on Linux 6.12, without root or sudo. All listings are genuine and unedited. Peer group numbers (98, 126) and mount IDs change between runs.
- The systemd, Docker and Kubernetes behaviour in the Notes comes from their documentation (Sources). It was not run here, because the test machine has no systemd.
